full_judgment:
Sometime in 1954 a Trust was created by a deed which provided for maintenance of certain public welfare institutions from the income of Chera Dangi Mela of Dinajpur. The trust was run by a committee selected by the local people for three years. The deed also provided for maintenance of accounts and its audit and procedures for holding of election of the next committee and measures for their infraction. Articles 23 and 36 are the two articles which cover this contingency. A detailed reference to them at this stage is not called for, because the question of jurisdiction of the District Judge is in question. The Committee was constituted sometime in 1976. Dispute arose regarding the finalisation of the accounts and its submission before the Mela Committee, and it is alleged that this led the local people to hold a meeting and pass a vote of no-confidence against the Mela Committee. The President of the Mela Committee was requested to have ad hoc committee appointed by the District Judge in terms of Article 36 of the Trust deed. The President filed an application before the District Judge, Dinajpur for the constitution of Ad hoc committee in terms of Article 36 read with Article 23 of the Trust deed which was registered as Miscellaneous Case No.17 of 1977. The question of jurisdiction of the District Judge to entertain the application arose when 17 members of the Mela Committee consisting of 26 members wanted to oppose the application by impleading them as defendants in the application. The District Judge observed that he was not acting as a District Judge but as persona designata and refused to implead them. He found that the Mela Committee had violated the terms of the trust deed, and so appointed three persons as-the members of the Mela Committee. Against this order a revision was taken by the present petitioner before the High Court under, section 115 of the Cede of Civil Procedure and a Single Judge upholding the view of the District Judge summarily rejected the revision petition. 

 7. Since we are confining to the question of the function of the District Judge in the context of the two clauses of the deed, we are refraining from entering into the facts in controversy. It is to be observed, the expression “District Judge”, has been used without any qualifying words. It is equally capable of being interpreted as a Court or a persona designata. If it is read as a court, it is found that under the Provisions of sections 73 and 74 of the Trust Act, the District Judge as the principal Court of the Civil Jurisdiction exercises substantially the same powers are mentioned in the deed. The two sections of the Trust Act read together clearly show that the sections confer a power of removal as well as the appointment of a trustee, if in the opinion of the Court a person is unfit or personally incapable to discharge the functions of a trustee. Section 73 relates primarily to the appointment of a new trustee and section 74 relates to a vacancy in the trusteeship and the disqualification of a trustee. These two sections further provide that the Court shall have regard apart from other considerations to the wishes of the author of the trust as expressed in the instrument of trust. The consequence of an action taken under any of the two sections is that the newly appointed trustee becomes vested with all the powers either solely or jointly with the continuing trustee as the case may be, and he will have the same power and authority as the trustee under the trust deed.
